solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Daughter in female toilets finds overflows

parts.note: standard abbreviation for female

indicators.note: the daughter sits in the toilets, so her letter goes inside the word for them

parts.note: British slang for toilets
standard abbreviation for daughter, placed inside the toilets

explanation.surface: A girl ducking into the ladies' room and finding the plumbing has burst.
explanation.walkthrough: The daughter lands between LOO and S; loo is the everyday British word for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Floods as a plural noun are cases of water spilling over, the same thing as overflows.

clue.text: Extremely useful anvil with a blue base

indicators.note: base in the sense of debased or corrupt, so the letters before it are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters; 'with' just joins the pieces

explanation.surface: A blacksmith praising a handy anvil that stands on a blue stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' reads as the anvil's stand, but it is the instruction to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something invaluable is worth more than any price could measure, hence of the greatest possible use.

clue.text: All the Americas wanting neologism encompassing Left

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so the coined word goes around the abbreviation for left

parts.note: a neologism is literally a newly coined term
standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A continent-sized appetite for fresh political vocabulary that includes the Left.
explanation.walkthrough: The L slips into NEW WORD just before its final D.
explanation.definitionFit: Europeans named North, Central and South America collectively the New World after Columbus's voyages.

clue.text: Usually game, cutting a deal

parts.note: the article kept as it stands

indicators.note: the game cuts into the deal, splitting it so it ends up sitting inside

parts.note: a sale is a commercial deal
Rugby Union, cutting the deal in half

explanation.surface: Someone who is normally up for it, getting involved in a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like an adjective meaning willing; it is the sport rugby union, splitting the deal in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe what normally happens in most cases, an adverbial synonym pair.

clue.text: Chap finished without European worker, almost

indicators.note: the word for finished goes without the European abbreviation, dropping that letter
almost means not quite complete, so the worker loses its final letter

parts.note: NEAT, in the sense of well finished or polished, minus E for European
HAND, a manual worker, with its last letter docked

explanation.surface: A man who has completed his job without the help of a continental labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means lacking rather than outside. Setters often clue a man's name with 'chap' or 'man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword convention lets any male first name be defined by a general word for a man or fellow.

clue.text: Point vessel around south

indicators.note: the vessel goes around the abbreviation for south, holding it inside

parts.note: a cup is a drinking vessel
compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: An instruction to aim a ship round towards the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship, but it is a drinking cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A cusp is a sharp tip where two curves meet, such as a pointed end on a tooth or moon.

clue.text: One asking old tax officials about new batch of papers?

indicators.note: the tax officials go about, that is around, the new batch of papers

parts.note: Inland Revenue, the former UK tax authority
standard abbreviation
a quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Someone querying the old taxmen about a fresh bundle of documents.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue was merged into HMRC in 2005, hence 'old'. The question mark nods to an inquirer also being a newspaper, a batch of papers.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquirer is a person who poses questions or investigates, literally one who asks.

clue.text: Connectors on back of mock paving bricks

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece written on another follows it, so the connectors come after
the back of a word is its final letter, so only the end of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of mock
things that link

explanation.surface: Parts fixed to the rear of a fake pavement.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only the last two words; 'back of' is a letter-picker, not the rear of the paving.
explanation.definitionFit: Klinkers are hard-fired Dutch-style bricks traditionally laid for roads and paths, a variant spelling of clinkers.

clue.text: Interminable slander associated with a graduate

indicators.note: without terminals, so the slander loses the letters at both of its ends

parts.note: CALUMNY with both end letters removed
the article as it stands

explanation.surface: Endless smears linked to a former student.
explanation.walkthrough: Calumny is a false, damaging statement; 'interminable' strips both its ends, not only the last.
explanation.definitionFit: An alumna is a female former student of a school or university, one who has graduated.

clue.text: Send over flower for increasingly bright star

indicators.note: sending something over flips it end to end, so the river is written backwards

parts.note: a flower is something that flows: here the English river Avon

explanation.surface: Delivering a bloom to someone whose fame is on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is a river, the thing that flows, here the Avon.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares up to many times its usual brightness before fading.

clue.text: Wishful pro freely displaying adoration

indicators.note: the preceding words are let loose, free to fall in any order

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A hopeful professional openly showing devotion to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Both fodder words sit together at the start, with the indicator right after them.
explanation.definitionFit: Worshipful describes feeling or expressing reverent devotion, which is what adoration is.

clue.text: I put into circulation leaderless paper run

definitions.note: a first-person riddle: the answer describes itself as one who puts things into circulation

indicators.note: a leader is a first letter, so the paper loses its opening letter

parts.note: TISSUE, a thin paper, minus its first letter
cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone boasting they distributed a newspaper with no editor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the answer: 'I' is the issuer describing itself, as a bank or state that issues money or stamps would.
explanation.definitionFit: An issuer is the body that releases currency, shares or stamps into general use.

clue.text: US idiot saving skin when bagging wrong hybrid borage variety

indicators.note: saving means except, so the idiot is taken except its skin, its outer letters
to bag is to put in a bag, so the stripped idiot holds the jumbled word

parts.note: KLUTZ, American slang for a clumsy fool, minus its first and last letters

indicators.note: a hybrid is a crossbred mix, so the word before it is mixed up

parts.note: anagram fodder, placed inside

explanation.surface: An American fool, trying to save face, while botching a cross-bred garden plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hybrid' looks botanical but is the anagram signal; 'when' just links the steps.
explanation.definitionFit: Lungwort, Pulmonaria, is a flowering plant belonging to the borage family, Boraginaceae.

clue.text: Complain feebly before vendor delivered accommodation for whites?

indicators.note: delivered as a speech is delivered, so the words are heard not seen

parts.note: to whine is to complain in a feeble, wheedling way
a vendor is one who sells

explanation.surface: Grumbling weakly ahead of a salesman's delivery of lodging for white laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just puts the first sound ahead of the second. 'Whites' are white wines, and the question mark flags that sly sense.
explanation.definitionFit: White wines are stored in a cellar, so it is literally the place that houses them.

clue.text: Options for patient old man close to Derby County

parts.note: pa, a father

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter of Derby is taken

parts.note: the final letter of Derby
Beds, short for Bedfordshire, an English county

explanation.surface: A father weighing up hospitals near Derby County's football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby County is a football club, but the words split: Derby supplies its last letter and County is Bedfordshire, abbreviated Beds.
explanation.definitionFit: In British NHS hospitals, pay beds are private places a patient can choose by paying fees.

clue.text: Don's bill affecting everyone that's neither positive nor neutral

indicators.note: the word loses both the positive and the neutral abbreviations it contains

parts.note: account, a bill

parts.words: affecting everyone that's neither positive nor neutral
parts.note: PANDEMIC, a disease affecting everyone, without P for positive and N for neutral

explanation.surface: A university lecturer's charge that applies to all, taking no stance either way.
explanation.walkthrough: The electrical abbreviations P and N are stripped from PANDEMIC; 'Don's' is possessive, so the answer is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A don is a university teacher, so anything belonging to one is scholarly, relating to university life.

clue.text: From the less weird version of Iron Maiden — only its first side?

indicators.note: keeping only the first part of the band's name means cutting off its closing stretch
a weird version is a strange rearrangement, so the letters are jumbled

parts.words: Iron Maiden — only its first side
parts.note: the heavy metal band's name with its final three letters dropped

explanation.surface: A fan preferring a tamer cover of a heavy metal record, having played just the A-side.
explanation.walkthrough: This is Latin, as in the argument a minori ad maius, from the lesser to the greater. 'First side' plays on a record's A-side.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin 'a' means from and 'minori' is the ablative of minor, the lesser, giving the literal translation.

clue.text: Minute blushing about how's your father, showing gloom no longer

parts.note: a mo, a moment

indicators.note: the blushing word goes about, that is around, the saucy euphemism

parts.note: pink-faced
British slang euphemism for sex, which is also 'it'

explanation.surface: Someone going briefly red over talk of sex, and cheering up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How's your father' is jokey British slang for sex, as is 'it'. 'No longer' marks the definition as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Morosity is an old-fashioned noun for sullenness, the state of being morose or gloomy.

clue.text: Dance, just missing opening record

indicators.note: the word lacks its opening, so its first letter goes

parts.note: HONEST, meaning just or fair, without its first letter
extended play record

explanation.surface: A dancer who barely missed the opening night of a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only' but is the adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-step is an early twentieth-century ballroom dance done in quick walking time.

clue.text: J A Wight is one desperate guy, sinking beers with Mike

indicators.note: the guy sinks the beers, taking them down inside him

parts.note: Desperate Dan, the strongman of the British comic The Dandy
ale is a type of beer
NATO alphabet word for M

explanation.surface: A famous author pictured as a hopeless man downing pints alongside a mate.
explanation.walkthrough: J A Wight wrote as James Herriot about vetting in the Yorkshire Dales. 'Desperate' belongs with 'guy' to make Desperate Dan.
explanation.definitionFit: Wight lived and worked in the Yorkshire Dales, so he is an example of a native or resident there.

clue.text: Film about working philosophical scholar

indicators.note: the film goes about, meaning around, the word for working

parts.note: a film of mist, a thin haze
on, as a machine switched on is working

explanation.surface: A movie about a thinker at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' is not a movie but a thin layer, as mist forms over a window.
explanation.definitionFit: A monist holds the philosophical doctrine that reality is ultimately one single substance or principle.

clue.text: Prejudice shown by warrant officer — watch it regularly being covered up

indicators.note: the selected letters are covered, wrapped inside the officer

parts.note: Regimental Sergeant Major, a warrant officer in the British Army

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, every other one of the phrase

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: An army officer's bigotry being hushed up while people are told to keep an eye on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Regimental Sergeant Major is the senior warrant officer of a British Army regiment; 'covered up' means the picked letters sit inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Racism is prejudice directed against people on the grounds of their race or ethnicity.

clue.text: Dangerous-waste container possibly making son cry

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement of the letters that follow

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A toxic bin that might reduce a boy to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure technical word, so the fodder is the only reliable route.
explanation.definitionFit: Synroc, synthetic rock, is a ceramic designed to lock up radioactive nuclear waste for storage.

clue.text: Broken nose seeing tissue regeneration

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the following letters are reassembled

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A fractured nose getting treatment to regrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing' looks like a link between wordplay and definition, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Neogenesis is the biological formation of new tissue, literally new creation, as in healing.

clue.text: Primarily gritty loam that is over waterlogged soil

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so each of the next two words gives its first letter

parts.note: first letters of gritty and loam

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned over, so the Latin phrase is written backwards

parts.note: id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A description of sandy earth lying on top of boggy ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' could mean placed on top, but here it reverses i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: Glei, or gley, is a sticky clay soil formed where the ground stays saturated with water.

clue.text: Note North-East Passage

parts.note: sixth note of the sol-fa scale
compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A remark about the Arctic sea route across the top of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the Northeast Passage, the Arctic shipping route; 'Note' is the sol-fa la.
explanation.definitionFit: A lane is a narrow way or path through which people pass.

clue.text: Frames note about affectation of superiority? Au contraire

indicators.note: one piece goes about the other, surrounding it
French for on the contrary, it swaps which piece does the surrounding

parts.note: putting on airs
second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Framed pictures annotated about snobbery, followed by a French shrug of disagreement.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the note goes about the airs; 'Au contraire' (French for on the contrary) reverses that, putting the airs about the note.
explanation.definitionFit: Airers are clothes horses, folding racks on which washing is hung to dry.

clue.text: Arch feature of out-of-bounds sex trade so regressive

indicators.note: out of its bounds means its boundary letters are gone, dropping both ends of the phrase

parts.note: SEXTRADE losing its first and last letters

indicators.note: regressing means going backwards, so the little word is written back to front

parts.note: taken as it stands, then turned backwards

explanation.surface: A newspaper-style swipe at a forbidden, backward-looking vice industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' looks like an adjective meaning knowing, but it is the architectural curve.
explanation.definitionFit: The extrados is the outer, upper curved surface of an arch, opposite the intrados underneath.
